# Computing Hecke Eigensystems of Hilbert-Siegel Cusp Forms

This paper presents an algorithm for computing the Hecke eigensystems of Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms defined over real quadratic fields with narrow class number one. The restriction to fields of narrow class number one provides a favorable arithmetic setting in which the necessary computations can be carried out explicitly, allowing us to develop a practical and effective computational approach to these otherwise intricate objects.

To demonstrate the algorithm in practice, we work through a series of illustrative examples over the real quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. This field serves as a natural testing ground, as it is one of the simplest real quadratic fields satisfying the narrow class number one condition, and it offers a concrete environment in which the various steps of the algorithm can be made explicit.

Through these examples, we are able to identify specific Hilbert-Siegel eigenforms arising within our computations. In particular, the explicit determination of Hecke eigensystems allows us to isolate individual eigenforms and to study their arithmetic properties in detail.

Among the Hilbert-Siegel eigenforms identified in this way, several are recognized as possible lifts originating from Hilbert eigenforms. This observation is of particular interest, as it suggests connections between Hilbert-Siegel modular forms and the more classical theory of Hilbert modular forms, and it points toward the presence of functorial lifting phenomena that merit further investigation.

# Computing Hecke Eigensystems of Hilbert-Siegel Cusp Forms over Real Quadratic Fields

## Introduction

The theory of automorphic forms occupies a central place in modern number theory, providing deep connections between arithmetic, geometry, and representation theory. Among the many families of automorphic objects, Hilbert-Siegel modular forms stand out as a natural generalization that combines two important directions: the passage from the rational numbers to totally real number fields (as in Hilbert modular forms) and the passage from genus one to higher genus (as in Siegel modular forms). Despite their theoretical importance, explicit computational data concerning these forms remains relatively scarce, particularly over base fields other than $\mathbb{Q}$.

This paper addresses this gap by presenting an algorithm for computing Hecke eigensystems of Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms defined over real quadratic fields with narrow class number one. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through explicit computations over the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$, the real quadratic field of smallest discriminant. A key outcome of our examples is the identification of Hilbert-Siegel eigenforms that appear to arise as lifts from Hilbert eigenforms, offering concrete evidence for and insight into the intricate lifting structures predicted by the Langlands philosophy.

## Background and Setup

Let $F$ be a real quadratic field with narrow class number one, a condition that ensures favorable arithmetic properties and simplifies the adelic description of the relevant automorphic forms. The assumption of narrow class number one guarantees, in particular, that we work with a single genus in the associated theory of quadratic forms and that strong approximation applies cleanly to our setting.

Hilbert-Siegel modular forms of genus $g$ over $F$ are automorphic forms for the symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}$ over $F$, generalizing classical Siegel modular forms (the case $F = \mathbb{Q}$) and Hilbert modular forms (the case $g = 1$). The Hecke eigensystems attached to these forms encode arithmetic information analogous to that carried by the Fourier coefficients of classical modular forms, and their computation allows us to probe the arithmetic of the underlying Galois representations and the network of functorial lifts relating different automorphic families.

## The Algorithm

Our computational approach relies on the theory of algebraic modular forms in the sense of Gross, which permits the calculation of Hecke eigensystems for forms whose associated archimedean representations are cohomological, by translating the problem into linear algebra on finite-dimensional spaces. Concretely, we exploit an exceptional isomorphism or a suitable definite inner form of the symplectic group, allowing us to replace the analytically complicated spaces of Hilbert-Siegel forms with combinatorially accessible objects.

The algorithm proceeds by:

1. **Constructing the relevant automorphic space.** We realize the space of cusp forms as a finite-dimensional vector space attached to a definite form of the symplectic group over $F$, using the narrow class number one hypothesis to control the class set.

2. **Computing Hecke operators.** For primes $\mathfrak{p}$ of $F$, we compute the action of the Hecke operators on this space via explicit descriptions of the corresponding double cosets, reducing the problem to enumerating lattices and neighbor relations.

3. **Diagonalizing the Hecke action.** By simultaneously diagonalizing the commuting family of Hecke operators, we extract the individual eigenforms and their eigensystems.

The narrow class number one condition on $F$ plays an essential role throughout, ensuring that the class set is manageable and that the arithmetic of the lattices involved remains tractable.

## Examples over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$

We apply our algorithm to the field $F = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$, which has narrow class number one and the smallest discriminant among all real quadratic fields. This makes it a natural first testing ground and one for which the computations remain feasible.

Our computations produce explicit tables of Hecke eigenvalues for Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ at small primes. Analyzing these eigensystems, we are able to identify certain eigenforms whose Hecke eigenvalues match those predicted for lifts constructed from Hilbert modular eigenforms. In particular, the observed relations among the eigenvalues are consistent with the eigenforms arising via known lifting constructions—such as Saito-Kurokawa type or endoscopic lifts—from lower-rank automorphic forms over the same base field.

The successful identification of these potential lifts serves two purposes. First, it provides a valuable consistency check on our algorithm, since the eigenvalues of genuine lifts satisfy predictable relations that we can verify independently. Second, and more importantly, it yields concrete data illuminating the structure of the space of Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms, distinguishing the lifted (non-tempered or endoscopic) part from the genuinely new forms that are expected to correspond to more interesting Galois representations.

## Conclusion

We have presented and implemented an algorithm for computing Hecke eigensystems of Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms over real quadratic fields of narrow class number one, and we have demonstrated its effectiveness through detailed examples over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. Beyond confirming the presence of eigenforms that are potential lifts from Hilbert eigenforms, our computations open the door to systematic exploration of these automorphic forms. Future work includes extending the computations to larger weights and levels, treating additional real quadratic fields, and comparing the resulting eigensystems with the predictions of the Langlands program, particularly regarding the associated Galois representations and instances of functoriality.

# Hecke Operators, Hilbert Modular Forms, and Siegel Modular Forms

The names **Hecke**, **Hilbert**, and **Siegel** are woven throughout the modern theory of modular and automorphic forms, a rich branch of number theory that connects analysis, algebra, and geometry. Each contributed foundational ideas that continue to guide research today.

## Hecke Operators

Erich Hecke (1887–1947) introduced a family of linear operators—now called **Hecke operators**—that act on spaces of modular forms. These operators are central because they can be simultaneously diagonalized, producing a basis of *Hecke eigenforms*. The eigenvalues of these operators encode deep arithmetic information: for instance, they appear directly in the coefficients of the associated *L*-functions.

Hecke's work revealed that modular forms possess a hidden multiplicative structure. When a modular form is an eigenform, its Fourier coefficients satisfy elegant recurrence relations governed by the Hecke eigenvalues. This insight established a bridge between the analytic world of automorphic forms and the arithmetic world of Galois representations, a theme that culminated in achievements such as the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

## Hilbert Modular Forms

While classical modular forms are defined on the upper half-plane and relate to the field of rational numbers, **Hilbert modular forms** generalize this theory to *totally real number fields*. Named in honor of David Hilbert, these forms live on products of several copies of the upper half-plane, acted upon by groups such as $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathcal{O}_K)$, where $\mathcal{O}_K$ is the ring of integers of a totally real field $K$.

Hilbert modular forms allow mathematicians to study arithmetic questions over more general number fields. They are essential tools in generalizations of the Langlands program and in the construction of Galois representations attached to automorphic representations over totally real fields.

## Siegel Modular Forms

Carl Ludwig Siegel (1896–1981) extended the theory in another direction, moving from one complex variable to **matrices of complex variables**. **Siegel modular forms** are defined on the *Siegel upper half-space*, consisting of symmetric complex matrices with positive-definite imaginary part. They are invariant under the action of the *symplectic group* $\mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z})$.

The integer $g$ is called the **genus** or **degree**; when $g = 1$, Siegel modular forms reduce to classical modular forms. These higher-degree forms are intimately connected to the geometry of **abelian varieties** and their moduli spaces, making them indispensable in both number theory and algebraic geometry.

## A Unified Perspective

Together, these three strands—Hecke operators, Hilbert modular forms, and Siegel modular forms—illustrate the remarkable unity of modern number theory:

- **Hecke** provided the algebraic machinery of operators and eigenforms.
- **Hilbert** pointed the theory toward general number fields.
- **Siegel** opened the door to higher-dimensional, symplectic generalizations.

All three feature prominently in the **Langlands program**, the vast web of conjectures that seeks to unify automorphic forms, Galois representations, and *L*-functions. Their combined legacy continues to inspire deep and active research, from explicit computations of eigenvalues to abstract questions about the arithmetic of algebraic varieties.

# Abstract

We present an explicit algorithm for computing Hecke eigensystems of Hilbert-Siegel cusp forms of genus 2 over real quadratic fields. Our approach exploits the theory of algebraic modular forms, following the framework of Gross, by working with definite quaternionic and orthogonal groups whose associated automorphic forms are conjecturally related to Hilbert-Siegel modular forms via the Jacquet-Langlands correspondence and theta lifts. By reducing the computation to linear algebra on spaces of functions supported on finite class sets of lattices, we obtain a method that circumvents the analytic difficulties inherent in working directly with Siegel modular forms over totally real fields.

The core of the algorithm involves enumerating genera of lattices over the ring of integers of a real quadratic field, computing the corresponding class sets via Kneser neighbor methods adapted to the totally real setting, and constructing Hecke operators through explicit lattice correspondences. We address the additional arithmetic complexity arising from nontrivial class groups and unit groups of the base field, and we describe optimizations that make the enumeration of neighboring lattices tractable in practice.

As applications, we tabulate Hecke eigenvalues for several examples over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$, and $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$, and we verify instances of predicted Galois representations and functorial lifts, including Saito-Kurokawa and Yoshida-type lifts. We further provide numerical evidence supporting conjectural congruences and paramodularity phenomena in the Hilbert-Siegel setting. Our implementation and data are made available to facilitate further investigation into the arithmetic of automorphic forms over totally real fields.

We develop and implement algorithms for computing Hilbert-Siegel modular forms of degree 2 over real quadratic fields with narrow class number one. Building on the theory of algebraic modular forms, we work with the definite quaternionic and orthogonal formulations that arise from the exceptional isogeny between the symplectic group $\mathrm{PGSp}_4$ and the special orthogonal group $\mathrm{SO}_5$. This framework allows us to realize spaces of Hilbert-Siegel eigenforms as spaces of automorphic forms on a compact-at-infinity form of $\mathrm{SO}_5$, where Hecke operators become tractable through the arithmetic of quinary quadratic lattices over the ring of integers.

By comparing computed eigenvalue systems against the predicted Satake parameters of these lifts, we distinguish genuine (non-lift) forms from those of endoscopic origin, providing numerical evidence for instances of the conjectural Langlands correspondence over $F$.

We conclude with tables of dimensions, sample eigenvalues, and several examples of eigenforms whose associated Galois representations are expected to be irreducible, offering data relevant to generalizations of the paramodular conjecture and to the study of abelian surfaces over real quadratic fields.
